cells.tense: What got imagined has been felt all the way through, and now it lives among people.
cells.act: find the rhythm and stay in it
cells.ask: Find the pace a regular shared thing can hold for a year — a dinner people count on, a weekly call, a small ritual — and keep to it, rather than the pace of one big push. Hold it there and add nothing.
cells.core:
In what's held in common here, something you pictured a while back has turned up whole — not finished, but felt through, and others are carrying it alongside you now. That's a different kind of full than getting it done. It sits close to ease, and it's shared, which are the same thing more often than not.

The speed you want to move at and the speed you actually move at are the same speed. That's rarer than it sounds and easy to break by pushing. Nothing needs building this week. Keep what you already carry feeling as alive as it felt at the start: settle on the pace it can hold past a season, stay there, and others will keep it with you because you keep it yourself. The next good thing gets made at that speed, or it doesn't get made at all.
cells.sheetLine: What you imagined has turned up whole, and it's ours now.
cells.verb: feeling an imagined thing through until it turns up whole in what's held in common

cells.tense: You're holding a shared thing in the shape you want it to be, and gripping harder than it grows.
cells.act: look after what grows with a steady hand
cells.ask: Choose a shared thing you tend — the group, the ritual, the thing people count on you for — and for seven days do only what keeps it fed. No improvements, no expansions, no fixing what nobody raised. If feeding it is hard to read, keep the one regular meeting and nothing else.
cells.core:
You've got a hand on a shared thing, and it's aimed at where the thing should be next year instead of where it is now. The care is doing something. So is the grip. People are getting bent toward a future version of it, and the version they're living in with you gets less of you than the plan does.

What grows doesn't need the next season this week. It needs tending now. For seven days do only what keeps the shared thing fed: no improvements, no expansions, no fixing what nobody raised. If that's hard to read, keep the one regular meeting and nothing else. Nothing here collapses from being left this small for a week. What a hard grip damages takes longer to see and longer to undo.

A shared thing will come to mind as you read this.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding it toward next year, not tending where it is.

cells.tense: You were part of the shared thing that held something, and you haven't been back in it since.
cells.act: hold two true things without declaring either
cells.ask: Name a gathering or regular thing you stopped attending. Go once and say nothing about where you've been. Carry what it stirs beside whatever you already believed about it, and leave the question open.
cells.core:
In shared things, the imagining that once had a room around it has gone quiet. You stopped turning up where something was being passed between people; what you made doesn't have a place now, and nothing has replaced it. Standing at a door that already closed is its own state, and it isn't where you currently live.

Don't repair the shared thing. Go stand inside one. Pick a gathering or regular thing you used to be part of and haven't been back to, and sit through it once. Nothing has to be settled about it while you're there. When it's over you'll have a read on it, and that read arrives in its own time. The sitting is the whole ask; what it shows you, it shows you.

You'll recognize the place as soon as you name it.
cells.sheetLine: The shared thing still exists. You left it behind.

cells.tense: You keep the shared thing running, and you don't count that as keeping it.
cells.act: sort what matters from what does not, carefully
cells.ask: Take the shared thing you keep up — a ritual you run, words you say, a gathering that stays on people's calendars — and write two columns: what it gives people, and what you put in. Draw no conclusion yet; the columns are the whole of it.
cells.core:
In what's held in common, something is being carried by more than you mean to admit. The people around it have drifted to the edge and manage it from there. It sits in your hands and gets described as the way it has happened. There's a hand on this, and the hand isn't the tradition's.

Look closely at a practice you keep up: separate what it gives people from what you put in. That's a distinction, made quietly, on paper, once. The second column may be most of it, or it may be nearly nothing and the thing has been flying without you. Both are worth having. Whether the hand stays or comes off is a question for another day; the columns are the work now, and any decision can wait until the page is done.

The page will show you what's actually being carried.
